_doc: T-3645: every evidence note a building's Details tab shows as its "Why" (tools/reading_notes.mjs), retold for younger readers. Keyed by the note's own words, since many claims share a note. Only the younger ages are written; no fact enters that the note does not hold, and the build's own talk (record ids, kit names, pixel and camera readings) is left out, so a young reader gets what was read and from where, and what is a guess.

8-10: An old writer says there was "a house and inclosed field north of the river, belonging to Mr. Coursoll." The map calls him "Mr Coursell." The writer Quaife says there were two Courselles. One was a well known trader. The only other sign of them in Chicago is their names in Kinzie's account books.
Sarony draws one small dark opening in the middle of the west end, just under the roof. It is built as a small window.

Eastman draws two small openings side by side on the east end, just under the roof. One is square and one has a round top. Both are built as small windows. The picture does not give their size. Eastman does not show the west end, so it has no windows.
There is one lodge in this group. It sleeps twenty people, by our rule. It is a camp of men who came on horses. They had lodges made of mats they carried, fire pits and lines for the horses.

It is 18.6 by 11.1 feet. That is the box drawn on the map, at forty feet to an inch. The drawing is a small picture of the roof and front, so the house could not be deeper. It is the smallest of the three houses, as Currey calls it "less pretentious," or plainer.
There are two lodges in this group. Each sleeps eight people, by our rule. It is a camp of men who came on horses. They had lodges made of mats they carried, fire pits and lines for the horses.
It is 75 feet tall. That number is written on the map along the pole. The rest of the map was sized from it.
A house where people lived. A writer named Quaife read Whistler's map. He says one of the houses was lived in by a soldier who had left the army. Which of the two houses it was is our guess.
The door is big enough to lead a horse through, like the town's other stables.

A walkway is open at both ends. Here each end is a gate between short bits of post wall. There was also a small door through the fort wall into the walkway. It is not built, because the map leaves the walkway out and shows no door there.
A worm fence is just split rails piled up in a zigzag. The picture draws rails, not boards.
A worm fence is just split rails piled up in a zigzag. It has no posts. Nothing is dug into the ground.
A worm fence is just split rails piled up in a zigzag. It has no posts.
It is about as tall as a rail. Both pictures draw the posts as high as the porch rail.
Both old pictures draw a fence of close pointed posts around the grass, not rails.
Both old pictures draw a roof that slopes two ways. Its top runs along the river, with a point at each end.
Both old pictures draw two chimneys coming up through the top of the roof, not at the ends.

Jean Baptiste Point du Sable built this house. Currey says he came from San Domingo and was a Black man. He traded with the Native people and lived here for over eighteen years. From 1804 it was John Kinzie's family home and the center of his trade. Wau-Bun calls it "the family mansion of my husband."

Currey wrote in 1912 that the Native people kept coming and going, as they always had. When they were near here, they lived in lodges by the river. Their favorite camp was on the south bank, near where the State Street bridge is now. A little stream ran into the river there, back to about where Randolph Street is now. The traders nearby watched for them. They wanted to trade goods for the furs the Native people brought. Currey tells us families came to trade all year and camped by the creek. That some lodges stood there on any one day is our guess.
Currey wrote in 1912 that a log cabin stood on this land. Some men who worked for Lee lived in it and ran the farm. He also calls it "the log house at Hardscrabble."
Currey says John Kinzie and his family lived here until he died in 1828. The only time they were gone was four years, from 1812 to 1816, when they had to leave. No people are shown here.
The map draws the flag pole lying down from the middle of the yard. It writes "75 feete" along it. The writer Quaife calls it "a lofty flagstaff."
Eastman draws a door near the right end of the front, and one window to its left. They are placed the way he spaces them.
Eastman draws its end wall in rows of logs, with the log ends sticking out at the corners. Later pictures from about 1831 show a light, smooth building here. The oldest picture is the one we follow.
Eastman paints the walls smooth and white. So we can't see what is under them. They are built of logs, like the rest of the yard and the house.
Eastman paints the walls white, next to the stable's dark logs. He painted it in 1820, eight years after 1812. It is the one picture of it, so we follow it.
Eastman's window lines up with the top of the door. It is about four fifths as tall as the door.
Eastman painted from the east. He shows the end of the roof toward us, with the back slope going off to the right. So the top of the roof runs east and west.

This was fitted to the old picture, not measured. The ends of the roof are cut back at a slant. That shape matched the picture best. It is steeper than the rest of the roof. That may be how the artist drew it.

The owner asked for the flag to fly. That is our guess. No record says the flag was up on 14 August 1812, the day before everyone left the fort. It flies on a nice day with a breeze from the south-west. Both of those are guesses too.

Forty feet by twenty-two. That size has no source here. An old article says Du Sable's bill of sale from 1800 gives the house as 22 by 40 feet. But we have not read that article, so the size is still a guess. It fits what our sources do say. Wau-Bun calls it a long, low house with four or five rooms in a row. Every picture shows a long front, about twice as long as the house is deep. The long side runs along the river.
Eastman's chimney stands a little left of the middle of the roof, as he sees the front.
Two old pictures show the chimney just inside the west end of the roof. We tried a few spots and checked them against the pictures. This spot fits both pictures best.

The old pictures show two chimneys. One is near the middle of the roof. The 1857 picture puts the other near the east end. Lossing puts his second one near the west end. Three of four pictures put it toward the east. So the 1857 places are used. Where Lossing's picture differs is written down.
Half of this was measured. The width, 12.2 feet, and where the front stands come from the map, which shows only the front. The map does not show how deep it was. The 10 feet of depth is our guess.

Half of this was measured. The width, 14.8 feet, and where the front stands come from the map. But the map only shows the front, with a round arch between two posts. It does not show how deep it was. The 10 feet of depth is our guess. That is short enough to stay clear of the building behind it.

Helm counts the people, not the lodges. He wrote that Captain William Wells came from Fort Wayne on 12 August with 27 Miami men. A meeting was held with the tribes there. There were about 500 warriors and 179 women and children.
Helm wrote that Captain William Wells came from Fort Wayne on 12 August with 27 Miami men. A meeting was held with the tribes there. There were about 500 warriors and 179 women and children.

Helm wrote that Captain William Wells came from Fort Wayne on 12 August with 27 Miami men. A meeting was held with the tribes there. There were about 500 warriors and 179 women and children. Wells came to lead the soldiers out of the fort. His Miami men marched with them on the 15th, some in front and the rest behind. No record we read says where they camped for the nights before. We guess it was somewhere near the fort.

The map calls this number 17, "Agents House." It was the house of the man who dealt with the Native people for the government. A writer named Quaife says two log houses stood a short way south-west of the fort. This was one of them.
The map calls this number 27, "Wharf of said River." It was the fort's landing on the Chicago River, where boats tied up.

The map writes "Comm'g Officers Garden" south of the fort. It shows eight beds in two rows. A magazine of 1857 tells of "the garden on the south side" of the first fort. A writer named Quaife says melons, fruit and vegetables grew there.

The old map writes "Worm Fence" along one side of the field. It draws a zigzag on three sides. So "worm fence" is the map's own word. The east side is drawn as a band of lines that runs down to the river bank. It is built as a worm fence too. We guess that the whole fence was one fence.

The map writes "a Sutlers Garden" here. A sutler sold goods to soldiers. It is the small plot east of the commanding officer's garden, toward the beach. A writer named Quaife tells of "a smaller garden" between the fort and the mouth of the river.

Measured from the old map. It is 17.3 by 19.0 feet, at the north-west corner of the fort. The map draws it with notched corners, sitting across both rows of posts. A writer named Quaife says the same. From the block houses, soldiers could watch outside the walls, and between the two rows of posts too.

Measured from the old map. It is 19.2 by 18.4 feet, at the south-east corner of the fort. The map draws it with notched corners, sitting across both rows of posts. A writer named Quaife says the same. From the block houses, soldiers could watch outside the walls, and between the two rows of posts too.

Measured from the old map. It is 22.1 feet long facing the yard and 13.3 feet deep. It is on the south side, west of the gate. Its back wall stands on the inner row of posts, like every building on the map.

Measured from the old map. It is 23.2 feet long facing the yard and 13.3 feet deep. It is on the south side, east of the gate. Its back wall stands on the inner row of posts, like every building on the map.
Measured from the old map. It is 24.8 feet long facing the yard and 11.9 feet deep. It has two rooms under one roof, as the map draws it.
Measured from the old map. It is 29.9 feet long on the side facing the open yard, and 13.3 feet deep. Its back wall stands on the inner row of posts, like every building on the map.
Measured from the old map. It is 43.8 feet long facing the yard and 12.2 feet deep. Its back wall stands on the inner row of posts, like every building on the map.
Measured from the old map. It is 5.5 by 7.7 feet. The map writes the number 16 upside down inside it.
Measured from the old map. It is 50.9 by 54.0 feet. It is the open yard that the buildings face.

Measured from the old map. It is 89.6 by 91.2 feet, between the inner edges of the fort walls. The back wall of each building stands on this line. On the map, the inner row of posts runs only between the buildings. Here the row goes all the way around, so behind the buildings the posts stand against their back walls.
There are marks at both ends of the roof on the map. They may be chimneys, like the ones on the agent's house. But they are too small to be sure.

No old record says what it was made of. Logs are our best guess. Every house here before 1812 that we know about was made of logs. A writer named Quaife calls two houses near the fort "two log houses."

This is not a measured height. We kept the old top point of the roof, about one meter above the walls. Now the roof is curved, not pointed. The curve, how far it sticks out and its edge are our guesses. They do not come from Whistler or Currey. What it is covered with, and its color, are guesses too. The old black and white picture shows none of them.
The map does not say. The soldiers built it out of local wood in 1803. The writer Quaife calls the two houses next to it "two log houses." The only brick building was the place for gunpowder.
The map does not say. The folded-up drawing shows a building more than one floor tall. A block house had to shoot over the two rows of posts, so it had to be tall.
The map does not say. It is made of wood, like every building at the fort. The one building made of brick was the place for gunpowder, says Quaife.
There is one door on the south side. It faces the back door of the house across the yard. There is one small window next to it. The pictures show only the west end and the roof.

A writer named Quaife says this walkway let the soldiers get to the water safely during an attack. So we think it was hidden behind walls. It is built as two rows of the fort's own pointed posts, with no roof. No record says it had a roof. No record says it did not.
The writer Quaife says the place for gunpowder was "a small structure made of brick." It was the only thing that did not burn when the fort was set on fire.
This is guessed by eye from the two old pictures. They are drawn at an angle, so the roof's slope cannot be measured.
This was worked out from Eastman's picture. The roof is about as tall as the wall. That makes it about forty degrees steep. The picture is small, and no number is given.

This was worked out from Sarony's picture. The porch roof is not very steep, about fifteen degrees. The main roof is steeper, about thirty degrees. The porch roof meets the main roof a little way in from the front wall.
Two old pictures show one chimney coming up through the top of the roof, near the west end. It was the chimney for the oven.
Two old pictures draw the chimney thin. It is about a third as wide as the end wall. That is an oven chimney, not a house chimney. No size is given.

Two old pictures show the top of the chimney just a little above the roof's peak. So it is set at about half a meter above it. That is eighteen inches, the height a town rule of 1835 asked for. It fits the pictures.
Sarony drew the end wall dark, with lines across it like rows of logs. He drew no other wall that way. The Teich painting shows it dark red-brown, the color old logs turn.
Measured against the door in the 1857 picture. Each window is about half as wide as the door.
Measured from the 1857 picture. The windows are tall, about two-thirds as tall as the door.
The chimney is moved to the front corner of the end wall. That is where it fits the 1912 picture. It also leaves room behind it for the shed the picture shows.
Where the soldiers lived. The west room held a store of food and goods. Whistler's list calls them numbers 12 and 13.
The fence is made of split wood boards on light posts.

The size comes from the map, but the shape is ours. The field is about 150 by 217 meters. That is about eight acres. The map says "Eight acres." A writer named Quaife says "eight or nine." The shape is a guess.
This is the box drawn on the old map, at forty feet to an inch. The drawing is only a small picture, so the real plan is our guess.

This is the box drawn on the old map, at forty feet to an inch. That is the scale the map gives for these houses. The drawing is a small picture of the roof and front together. So the box is the biggest the house could be, and the real plan is our guess.

This is the box drawn on the old map, sized at the map's own scale of forty feet to an inch. The drawing is a small picture of the roof and front together. So the box is the biggest the house could be. The real floor plan is our guess. The long side runs along the front, north to south.

This is the box drawn on the old map, at forty feet to an inch. The drawing is a small picture of the roof and front together. So the box is the biggest the house could be, and the real plan is our guess. The long side runs north to south. It is drawn 29 by 47 feet, the bigger of the two. That fits a trading store with rooms to live in.
This box is sized at the scale of the garden next to it, fifty feet to an inch. This plot gives no scale of its own, so its size is our guess.

This is the shape drawn on the old map, made bigger to fit its place. The map has no scale near the field. So its size comes from how much the river bank was stretched. It is about 31 by 18 meters, or about 560 square meters. The map draws a slanted shape, but the fence here is a box. The box is a bit short on one side. That way the fence stays north of Le Mai's house. The map puts his house just outside the fence. The field is small. The map maker squeezed the land outside the fort, so the size is as unsure as the place.

The flag's look comes from the law, not from anyone who saw it. No record tells us what the first fort's flag looked like. But an American fort flew the American flag. A law of 1794 said the flag had fifteen stars and fifteen stripes. That law lasted until 1818. So every day from 1803 to 1812 used that flag. How the stars were laid out, how big it was and how worn it was are our guesses.

The years here are a guess. They start on 25 January 1808. That is the date on Whistler's drawing, the one day we know the field had a fence. It may be older. We guess it still stood in August 1812, but no record says so after the drawing. The Courselles show up at Chicago only in Kinzie's account books. The years end on 16 August 1812, when the fort burned and the people around it left. A worm fence is just a pile of rails. No one says anybody kept it up while the place stood empty for four years. So it ends then.

These dates are the whole year, not dates for these lodges. Currey says the Potawatomi came and went, camping by the river, in the years before the war. He gives no date for any one lodge. So this camp stands for that habit. It is shown every day of 1812. It is never shown in 1835.

The map draws the edge of the field as a dotted line, not as a fence. So the fence is our guess. This was a corn field next to a cattle seller's house and the fort's hay field. It had to keep animals out. Whistler had a post fence near the fort taken down and replaced by "a common rail fence." The map also calls the zigzag fence around Coursoll's field a "Worm Fence." A common rail fence is a worm fence.

We know the haystacks were here on one day. The book Wau-Bun says haystacks stood with the cattle across from Lee's cabin on 7 April 1812. That was the day the war party came. Those were the winter's stacks. The stacks shown in August are a guess. We guess the farm cut hay again in July 1812. No record says anyone worked the farm after April. The stacks end on 16 August 1812, when the fort burned. Charles Lee, his son and everyone in his house but his wife and baby were killed on the 15th. No one fed animals at Lee's Place after that.
The 1857 picture shows a rail with little posts between the porch posts. It is open at the door.
A picture from 1857 shows six posts across the front. Lossing's picture shows fewer, thicker ones, but it is smaller. So there are six, from the clearer picture.
The 1857 picture shows plain windows with dark glass. There are no shutters beside them.

The 1857 picture shows two windows on each side of the door, under the porch. In Lossing's picture the porch is dark and shows none. Wau-Bun says the house had four or five rooms in a row. The front was long enough for each room to have a window.
The 1912 picture shows a dark roof that slopes two ways. Its top runs along the river side. The picture was made long after, so this is a guess from it.

The 1912 picture shows a lower shed past the chimney, at the end up the river. Its face is drawn in up and down lines, like boards. So it is built as a board shed leaning on the end wall, behind the chimney. The picture's angles for it do not match the house, so its size is only a rough guess.

The 1912 picture draws a zigzag rail fence along the river bank and around the field. That is a worm fence. The picture was made long after, so this is a guess from it. It is also the kind of fence a far-off farm built when it had no tool to dig post holes.
The 1912 picture puts the chimney outside the left end, as seen from the river. That is the end up the river.

The camp of the Potawatomi who came to Chicago in August 1812, before the soldiers left the fort. The book Wau-Bun tells of their camp on the south side of the river. Currey says groups of lodges stood along the creek on 14 August. Captain Heald wrote that they came for the goods in the fort's store. The meeting of the 12th was held with them. The old books do not say whose lodge was whose. Wau-Bun names one woman, the wife of a chief from the Illinois River, at one lodge. No lodge here is given to a family or a person.
The map draws a roof that slopes two ways over the house. It draws the same roof on the agent's house and the store. So that is the roof used for all of them.
The map draws a roof that slopes two ways. All the houses on this side of the river have one.
The map draws one chimney, against the west end of the house.
The fence goes around a space 46 meters wide and 16 meters deep. That is a kitchen garden for a family and its workers.
The field of Lee's farm. Captain Heald puts the cabin "in a field on the Portage branch." Currey says a man named Charles Lee owned some farm land here.

The first of three small buildings in a row, south of the agent's house. The map writes the number 24, "Stables," next to the row. It does not say which of the three it means. So all three are built as stables.
The fort's own field. The map from January 1808 calls it the Company Garden and public Cornfield. A man named Quaife read the map and says the same.
The fort's flag pole, in the middle of the open yard.
The fort's gunpowder store. Whistler's list calls it number 4.
This group's patch of ground is 30 by 24 meters. The lodges, yards and things are laid out inside it, with open ground between them. How big the patch is was made up.
This group's patch of ground is 36 by 26 meters. The lodges, yards and things are laid out inside it, with open ground between them. How big the patch is was made up.
This group's patch of ground is 36 by 28 meters. The lodges, yards and things are laid out inside it, with open ground between them. How big the patch is was made up.
The notes say "shingled Roofs." Each building's drawing shows a roof that slopes two ways, with the top line running along the building. So that is the roof used here.
The inner of the two rows of pointed posts around the first fort. The writer Quaife says the block houses could watch outside the walls, and between the two rows of posts too.
How new or worn the mats are. New ones are fresh and golden. Old ones have turned gray from years of being carried and rained on. Some groups have both. Which group has which is our choice.
How new or worn the mats are. Which group has which is our choice.
The outer of the two rows of pointed posts around the first fort. The writer Quaife says the block houses could watch outside the walls, and between the two rows of posts too.
The open yard that the buildings face. The writer Quaife says a tall flag pole stood in the middle of it.
The same notes say the porches faced the open yard. So they are built on that side. No one says how deep the porch was or how it was held up. So this is a usual porch.

The old 1808 drawing clearly shows one chimney on this building, so one is built. We guess it was still there in 1812. No hidden chimney is added. Where it stood, how tall it was and what it was made of are our guesses.

The old 1808 drawing clearly shows one chimney on this building, so one is built. We guess it was still there in 1812. No hidden chimney is added. Where it stood, how tall it was and what it was made of are our guesses. There may have been more that the drawing does not show.

The old 1808 drawing clearly shows two chimneys on this building, so two are built. We guess they were still there in 1812. No hidden chimney is added. Where they stood, how tall they were and what they were made of are our guesses. There may have been more that the drawing does not show.

The old 1808 drawing clearly shows three chimneys on this building, so three are built. We guess they were still there in 1812. No hidden chimney is added. Where they stood, how tall they were and what they were made of are our guesses. There may have been more that the drawing does not show.

The last of three small buildings in a row, south of the agent's house. The map writes the number 24, "Stables," next to the row. It does not say which of the three it means. So all three are built as stables.
This year's hay, cut and piled in July 1812. It is pale. The top is a bit darker where it was raked to keep the rain off.
Two lodges made of mats. One is a winter house, like the one Forsyth tells of. The other is what a family on the move carried.
No one wrote this down. The drawing is too small to show it.

No one wrote down its size. The shape comes from a picture of 1912. It shows a long, low house. The river side is about two and a half times as long as the end. It has three doors and six windows. So the house is 48 by 18 feet. The picture was made long after, and it gives no sizes, so the size is ours. A log house this long was likely two rooms under one roof. Here it is built as one.

No one wrote this down, and this is not what the picture shows. The doors in the picture are only about 1.5 meters tall. That is too low for a man to walk under. So the doors are built 1.7 meters tall, a low cabin door.
No one wrote this down. It is the same as the second fort's.
No one wrote this down.

No one wrote this down. The field is 150 by 90 meters, about three acres. That is big enough to grow food for a fort. Currey says the farm's crops sold well at the fort. The picture's field is wide. No record gives its size or edges.
No one wrote this down. It is a box of logs, the one kind we can build. That was a usual way to build a dock of logs on a river bank.

No one wrote this down. The roof slopes two ways, with a point at each end. The old drawing of the first fort shows its log houses outside the wall with roofs like this. So that is the roof used here.

No one wrote this down. Each stack is round and about twelve feet across. Two or three men could pile one up in a day. In Wau-Bun, two people walking around the stacks were hidden by them, so they had to be this big. The four stacks are a little different in size, as stacks made by hand are.
No one wrote this down. It is a fence of split boards.
No one wrote this down. The gate is as wide as a path. It is the narrowest gate we can build.
No one wrote this down. The log walls go up about eight feet to the roof. That is how tall a one-room house usually was.
No one wrote this down. The log walls go up about eight feet to the roof. That is how tall a one-room house usually was. The map gives no height.
No one wrote this down. It is about four and a half feet tall. That is how tall a worm fence had to be to keep animals out.
No one wrote this down. It is about four and a half feet tall. That is how tall a worm fence had to be to keep farm animals out of a field. The fort's own fields here have fences that tall.
No one wrote this down. The log walls are about seven feet tall. That is a little lower than its neighbors, because it is the smallest house on this side of the river. The map gives no height.
No one wrote this down. The walls are about ten feet tall. The pictures draw the porch posts almost as tall as the wall. A porch roof needs room to stand under it.
No one wrote this down. The shed goes back 1.8 meters from the chimney. That keeps it close to the picture, and leaves room for a small shed.
No one wrote this down. The posts are close together, as both pictures draw them.
No one wrote this down. It is five feet tall. That is enough to keep farm animals out of a garden.
No one wrote this down. There are four rails, one on top of the next. The fort's corn field by the river fork has the same. Cows were near, so the fence had to be tall.
No one wrote this down. Each part of the fence steps out from the line a little. That makes the zigzag. Three feet was the usual step.

No one wrote this down. This stack is lower than the other three. It is the one left from the winter. The cows had been fed from it, and it had sunk down. In April, the men in Wau-Bun pulled hay from stacks like this for the cattle.
No one wrote this down. It has one more rail than the light fence around the fort's garden in 1830. That is because it is next to a cattle seller's field.
No one wrote this down. There is one chimney at the end. A family by the lake needed at least that much for winter. No record says where it was.

No one wrote this down. There is one gap on the river side. It leads to the place where canoes landed below the cabin. The farm got to the fort by river. Currey says people usually went between the farm and the fort by canoe.
No one wrote this down. It has one floor with space under the roof above it. That is the least a farm family needed at a fort far from town.
No one wrote this down. The porch is seven feet deep. That is about a third as deep as the house in the pictures.
No one wrote this down. The fence is made of split wood boards on light posts.
No one wrote this down. The drawing is not to size. It was a small building for gunpowder, one floor high.
No one wrote this down. The folded drawings are not drawn to size. So we do not use them for how steep the roof is. The second fort's buildings have the same roof.
No one wrote this down. The picture draws about four rails in each part. A field fence for cows needs more rails than a garden fence's three.
No one wrote this down. The picture draws the shed's roof steeper than the house's. So it is set at 45 degrees, which fits the picture.
No one wrote this down. The six windows in the 1912 picture are each a little under one meter wide.
No one wrote this down. The three doors in the 1912 picture are each a little over a meter wide. So they are built 1.2 meters wide.
No one wrote this down. The windows in the 1912 picture are about 0.8 meters tall. Their tops line up with the tops of the doors.
No one wrote this down. Each part of the fence steps out three feet. That was the usual zigzag.

No one wrote this down. The posts are twelve feet tall. That is the second fort's height, and a usual height for a fort wall. The map maker says some posts were "five feet in length." But those were for a fence across the river that he took down.
No one wrote this down. It has two floors of logs, 5 meters tall, like the second fort. The folded drawings do not agree with each other, so their heights are not used.
No one wrote this down. It has two floors of logs, like the block house of the second fort. The folded drawings are not drawn to size.
No one wrote this down. It is a wood pole.
No one wrote this down. The door is tall enough to lead a horse through.
No one wrote this down. The walls are under seven feet tall. The pictures show a low building.
No one wrote this down. It is a bake house, one floor high.
No one wrote this down. It is a shop, one floor high.
No one wrote this down. It is a small house, one floor high.
No one wrote this down. It is a stable, one floor high.
No one wrote this down. The boards are close enough to keep a pig out.
No one wrote this down. No old record tells us about the roof.
No one wrote this down. This is the narrowest gate we can build.
No one wrote this down. The map draws every building on this side of the river in logs.
No one wrote this down. The drawing on the map is too small and too rough to tell how steep the roof was.
No one wrote this down. The roof on the map is just a little picture, so it does not show how steep the roof was.
No one wrote this down. The roof is as steep as the houses next to it. The map's drawing is too small and too rough to tell.
No one wrote this down. The roof is as steep as the other houses on the north side.

The book Wau-Bun tells of a long, low house with a porch along its front, in 1831. Currey says Kinzie bought the house in 1804, fixed it up and added a porch. Neither says the porch was there before August 1812. Lossing's picture shows the house next to the first fort with a porch. So the porch is built here.

The book also says the family had plenty of food from the garden, the corn field and the dairy. They gave kegs of butter to the ship captains.
Whistler calls these three houses the Oather Dwelling Houses. That means other houses. Currey says this one was a plain little cabin. It was the home of Antoine Ouilmette.

Whistler's list says the fort had "2 Port Holes for Cannon" and "3 Loop Holes for small arms." The writer Quaife says the cannon were in the block houses. Where those holes were is not marked on the map. So where the slits are, and how high, is our guess.
Whistler's map marks "Block Houses" as number 1. They are drawn at two corners of the fort, the north-west and the south-east. The writer Quaife says the same thing.
Whistler's list calls this number 11. It is on the west side. A writer named Quaife says the lower officers lived here. It was across from the other houses.

Whistler's list calls the east room "Soldiers Barracks." It calls the west room "Contractors Store," a store of food and goods. The writer Quaife says the same. It is built as one building. The store is just a room, and we do not build the insides of rooms.
Whistler's notes say the soldiers' houses were two floors high. They had wood shingle roofs, and porches facing the open yard. The writer Quaife read the same map and says the same.

The old 1808 drawing shows four windows on each floor, in a row. From left to right they go short, short, tall, short. Where they sit is only a rough guide. Their sizes are our best guess. One tall opening on the ground floor is built as a door. That does not mean it was a door. The tall windows upstairs are built as glass windows, not as doors to the porch. Nothing else about the building was changed.
